item.title: ESPN personality Chris Canty shares wildly inaccurate statement about Ole Miss football on 'First Take'
item.description: Chris Canty claimed Ole Miss had just two AP Top 10 wins in 60 years on "First Take," but the Rebels have 16 such wins since 2000 alone.
item.content:encoded:
With Week 3's showdown between LSU and Ole Miss delivering on every single level, talking heads were still reacting to the Rebels' 32-24 win over the Tigers on Tuesday morning. Given that it was one of the most highly anticipated college football games in recent history, taking a few days to dissect it all is well warranted, but if you're going to do so, you have to have the most basic facts correct.

ESPN did not abide by that rule.

'First Take' host Stephen A. Smith was joined by former NFL players Jeff Saturday and Chris Canty to discuss Ole Miss quarterback Trinidad Chambliss and what his future in the league could look like. While Canty dropped compliment after compliment about Chambliss and his abilities, one statement he made about Ole Miss' history as a program was not even close to being accurate.

"Ole Miss has had two wins against AP Top 10-ranked teams in the last 60 years, and that dude has both of them," Canty said while pointing to a graphic of Chambliss.

While we can say that Canty is being a prisoner of the moment and also understand that he was likely fed that 'statistic' about the Rebels by a producer or researcher at ESPN, we can also recognize just how far detached from reality it is.

MISSISSIPPI GOV TROLLS LANE KIFFIN, LSU AFTER OLE MISS DEFEATS TIGERS IN COACH'S RETURN TO OXFORD

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

As Canty noted, Chambliss led Ole Miss to a win over LSU on Saturday and against Georgia in last year's College Football Playoff, giving him two wins over AP Top 10 teams, but he and the program have accomplished that feat many, many more times than two.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Just last season, No. 4 LSU visited Ole Miss and Chambliss led the Rebels to a 24-19 win. In 2024, Jaxson Dart pushed the Rebels past No. 3 Georgia. Ten years earlier, Ole Miss beat No. 3 Alabama 23-17 and No. 4 Mississippi State six weeks later, before beating the Crimson Tide on the road the following year when Bama was the No. 2 team in the nation.

Since the turn of the 21st century alone, Ole Miss has beaten 16 teams ranked inside the AP Top 10.

Mistakes happen, but some are far more egregious than others, and Canty's certainly falls into that category.

item.title: Bull elk in Colorado nicknamed 'Smash' is chasing off trucks and golf carts
item.description: A bull elk named Smash terrorizes golf carts and trucks during elk rutting season in Estes Park, Colorado, and video captures the wild chase.
item.content:encoded:
If you're golfing in Estes Park, Colorado this time of year on the territory belonging to a bull elk nicknamed "Smash," do not let up on the accelerator pedal of your golf cart.

He's not much of a fan of vehicles in general and will give chase if you're too close for comfort. Over the last several days of what is the middle of elk rutting season, he's been out making his presence known.

Last week Smash put his head down and attempted to live up to his name by charging at the side of a maintenance truck.

MOOSE WANDER ONTO NORTH DAKOTA HIGH SCHOOL GOLF TOURNAMENT COURSE, CAUSING AN UNFORGETTABLE DELAY

He then set his sights on a golf cart in a video captured by Good Bull Guided and captioned, "Smash was at it again tonight! He takes being a golf hazard pretty seriously!"

He's a fan favorite and can be heard being cheered on by those capturing the video. Nothing says fun in Estes Park, Colorado quite like a bull elk chasing anything with wheels.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

For anyone questioning either the elk's nickname or his frustration with vehicles, these were not just recent occurrences.

Smash has chased golf carts off before, and even caught one with a quick smack from his antlers around this time last year.

If you have to test your luck in a golf cart near him, I'd keep it moving. Don't even think about applying the brakes until you're sure he's given up.

You've been thoroughly warned by Good Bull Guided, "Anything on wheels better watch out for Smash!" That bull elk doesn’t appear to be playing around.

His antlers are locked and loaded this time of year. If he has to use them on other bull elk, maintenance trucks or even golf carts, he will.

item.title: Deadly helicopter crash kills 2 pilots battling raging wildfire in Yosemite
item.description: The FAA and NTSB are investigating the Precision Helicopters crash that killed two pilots battling the Dome Fire wildfire in Yosemite National Park. So far, the cause of the crash is a mystery.
item.content:encoded:
Two pilots were killed when a firefighting helicopter crashed while battling a wildfire in Yosemite National Park.

The helicopter went down while conducting water bucket drops on the Dome Fire on Sunday, according to The Associated Press (AP).

The pilots were the only people aboard the aircraft. They worked for Precision Helicopters, a company contracted to support the firefighting operation, the AP reported.

'WE THOUGHT WE WOULD DIE': PASSENGERS THROWN INTO CEILING DURING TERRIFYING FLIGHT

The deceased pilots were later identified as Ryan Cutter and Greg King, according to social media posts from Precision Helicopters.

Cutter had been a helicopter pilot since 2011, including a year-and-a-half with Precision Helicopters, according to his LinkedIn profile. He was described as a "deeply loved husband, son, friend and godfather" on GoFundMe.

King had previously worked on wildland fires in Alaska and extensively alongside the Alaska Division of Forestry & Fire Protection, according to a statement from the agency.

The agency said King had close ties to its wildland firefighting community, including loved ones who currently work for the division.

"Greg was a dedicated aviator and a dear friend to many of us," the agency said. "We are mourning both pilots who bravely supported firefighting efforts, and our hearts go out to their families."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Precision Helicopters also paid tribute to Cutter and King in a social media post following the crash.

"These two men brought honor to the mission. Their dedication and service will never be forgotten," the company wrote.

The Super Puma helicopter was using a water bucket to help suppress the Dome Fire when it crashed near a lake, Benjamin Cossel, a spokesperson for the Federal Complex Incident Management Team overseeing the firefighting response, told AP.

The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the crash, with the NTSB leading the investigation, according to the FAA.

The crash occurred as hundreds of firefighters continued working to contain the Dome Fire, which started on Sept. 15 near Wawona, California.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

About 580 personnel were battling the wildfire, which had burned roughly 4.7 square miles and was about 15% contained, the AP reported.

The crash site was southeast of Ostrander Lake, about seven miles northeast of Wawona and roughly nine miles south of Yosemite's El Capitan, according to the AP.

A procession carrying the two deceased helicopter pilots was seen traveling through Merced on Monday, Sept. 21, according to Fox 26 in California. 

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Writing on Facebook about the somber procession shown on video, one user said, "Prayers for their families and loved ones. May they rest in peace."

Another said, "They paid the ultimate price for all of us. May God bless their families."

The Associated Press contributed reporting.

item.title: Jaxson Dart knee injury evaluation continues with serious possibility he may miss the remainder of the season
item.description: Jaxson Dart may need surgery on his MCL sprain, with a season-ending absence not ruled out as the New York Giants await a crucial second opinion.
item.content:encoded:
The possibility Jaxson Dart may miss the rest of the New York Giants season has not been ruled out, a source confirmed to Outkick on Tuesday, as medical evaluations continue on the New York Giants quarterback's left knee.

Dart, his doctors and the team will determine next steps for addressing the knee injury he suffered Monday night, early in the game, against the Los Angeles Rams.

The source declined to say why Dart could miss the season. That outcome, however, would become likely if Dart requires surgery for a detached MCL ligament — a procedure that could carry a recovery timeline of four to five months.

GIANTS QUARTERBACK JAXSON DART SUFFERS KNEE INJURY AGAINST RAMS, MCL ISSUE FEARED

New York Giants coach John Harbaugh was not ready to go that far on Tuesday during his day-after press conference.

"I'm not sure exactly what news or anything's been stated, but right now, evaluations are ongoing," Harbaugh said. "We haven't got any final decisions yet. We've learned a lot more.

"I wouldn't really want to share too much until decisions get made. That takes more than one person, takes everybody involved. So when we know, you know, what direction we're gonna have to go or whatever it might be."

Harbaugh will meet with Dart (again) after he gets a second opinion on the MRI test he underwent on Tuesday. Then a decision on what to do next will be made in conjunction with the medical experts and Dart.

"So, I don't want to get out over our skis on that," Harbaugh said.

OutKick first reported on Monday night that Dart had suffered a sprained MCL and would miss time.

Asked after the game about his quarterback and reports of an MCL sprain, Harbaugh said the reports were in the correct "neighborhood."

That was after ESPN reported general manager Joe Schoen told sideline reporter Laura Ruthledge that Dart "will be OK."

That may still be true.

GIANTS' JAMEIS WINSTON HAS SKY-HIGH HOPES AFTER HIRING JOHN HARBAUGH WITH JAXSON DART'S EMERGENCE

But it might take a long while.

What is certain is that Dart isn't playing anytime soon and definitely not Sunday against the Tennessee Titans.

Jameis Winston becomes the Giants' new starting quarterback for the time being. The club will also likely promote Jake Haener from the practice squad to serve as a backup, and they may even add Brandon Allen.

This is obviously terrible for the Giants and seemingly derails their season, even after only two games.

It's as if this team is cursed. Consider that in recent years the club has dealt with significant, if not season-ending, injuries to Dart, receiver Malik Nabers, running back Cam Skattebo, left tackle Andrew Thomas, and even running back Saquon Barkley years ago.

This is not a spotlight shining on injuries because the Giants play in New York.

item.title: Sturgill Simpson says talent is 'not as rare as people think' and work ethic matters more
item.description: Sturgill Simpson ripped entitled singers with no work ethic, revealing what he says separates lasting careers from those flushed by the machine.
item.content:encoded:
Sturgill Simpson doesn't think there's a hidden secret to success in music.

Simpson has carved out an incredibly loyal following in the country music industry by singing largely outlaw country tunes.

However, that's far from his only skill. He also released a pair of albums under his alter ego Johnny Blue Skies.

‘YELLOWSTONE’ STAR LUKE GRIMES REVEALS OUTLAW COUNTRY WAS 'NO-GO' IN PASTOR FATHER’S HOUSE

His secret to success?

Just work hard.

Simpson spoke with Playboy about his rise in the music industry, and he took some not-so-subtle shots at people who don't think they need to earn it.

"I had all the thankless f***ing jobs. There are so many people I met when I moved to Nashville 15 years ago who had exponentially more talent than I do, but they had no work ethic. Or they thought [sic] that, because they were brilliant, they didn’t have to earn their medals," Simpson told Playboy (via Whiskey Riff).

He continued, "No, b*tch, get in the van and go do circles and sleep on f***ing floors for six months until 12 people in a room give a sh*t. That’s the only thing that’s going to be lasting. If you’re waiting on some machine to pump you out, that machine is going to flush your a** too. Talent’s not as rare as people think."

Simpson's comments shouldn't come as a surprise to anyone. This is the man who famously once said he was "plotting" the "destruction" of the music industry. Or, that's certainly how his comment was interpreted.

He's nothing if not honest and straight to the point. That's the authenticity that has gained him millions of fans.

The Kentucky-born country singer also does more than just sing. He does some acting, and appeared in the legendary HBO show "The Righteous Gemstones" to sing a cover of "All the Gold in California." It's 100% worth checking out online because it's hilarious and also impressive.

item.title: DAVID MARCUS: In deep blue Minnesota a red dawn may be rising ahead of the midterms
item.description: Minnesota's GOP candidates Michelle Tafoya and Lisa Demuth are closing in on Democratic Party rivals as a billion-dollar fraud scandal fuels outrage.
item.content:encoded:
Six months ago, very few people imagined that this year’s senate and governor races in Minnesota would be anything but Democratic Party blowouts, but as we approach October, and the beating heart of the midterms, the Gopher state appears suddenly and stunningly in play.

Recent polling, as shoddy as this cycle’s surveys have been, show GOP senate candidate Michelle Tafoya within 2 or 3 points of her opponent, sitting Lt. Gov. Peggy Flannagan, and while the chaos surrounding the death of Alex Pretti at the hands of ICE is in the rearview mirror, the massive Somali fraud scandal decidedly is not.

On Sunday, I headed over to Cowboys Saloon in Lexington, Minn., just north of the Twin Cities, to attend a Vikings game watch party for local Republican volunteers, where I found Lisa Demuth, Speaker of the Minnesota House and candidate for governor, rallying the troops ahead of some door knocking and leafleting.

LEE CARTER: THE SUMMER POLLS MISSED THE POINT: VOTERS ARE MOVING — AND THE MIDTERMS BEGIN

Demuth is running against sitting senator Amy Klobuchar for governor as the Minnesota Democrats play a high stakes game of political musical chairs, in which poor Gov. Tim Walz has already lost his seat.

"We have heard from Minnesotans across the state," Demuth told Fox News Digital, "when we’ve been traveling, that they are ready for a change, it's nice to see the polling start to reflect that, but we were hearing voters ready for a change, ending fraud, making the state affordable, just all the desperate change we have needed."

Minnesota’s GOP House Majority Leader, Harry Niska, was also on hand for the 9-3 Vikings victory and offered this explanation to the tightening races: "It’s not a surprise to those of us who have spent months talking to voters in Minnesota as more and more Minnesotans become aware of the billions of dollars that have been stolen from our taxpayers."

'WE HAVE NOT SLOWED DOWN': MINNESOTA NOT OUT OF THE WOODS ON MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL, EXPERT WARNS

The fraud that Niska refers to is, of course, the ongoing scandal surrounding the Minneapolis community in the Cedar Riverside neighborhood, that has been bilking tax dollars with fake learning centers and autism care, to the tune of a possible $9 billion, with a "B," dollars.

Indeed, the scandal, now long since a national story, was on the tongues of almost everyone I spoke to, of both parties, in the warm afterglow of the Vikings "W" once the canvassers had left to knock upon doors.

MINNESOTA'S ANTI-ICE AID FUND BECOMES LATEST CASUALTY OF STATE'S EMBARRASSING FRAUD PROBLEM

"It’s infuriating," Tony, in his late 30s, told me, going on to say, "There’s just no rules, and we all pay for it, it's like, how does this even happen?"

I met Bill and Laura, who appeared to be longtime friends over a cigarette and they had two distinct takes on the races. Bill told me of Michelle Tafoya, "She doesn’t impress me," then suggested, "I just don’t see the makings for an office for [her]."

WALZ APPROVAL RATING CRATERS TO LOWEST LEVEL EVER AND TRAILS TRUMP AMID MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL: 'TIRED OF IT'

But, when I asked how Minnesotans were feeling about their leadership on the state and federal level, it was Laura, without a beat who insisted, "We’re all very discouraged," prompting Bill to admit that Walz, "Took the opportunity to make choices that were not well conceived."

In one dire last comment, Laura shook her head and said, "People are losing hope, man."

My longest conversation of the day was with Dan, a smart, well-traveled and worldly man with a lovely little dog named Jasper.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Dan is a Democrat who freely acknowledges that bad mistakes have been made by Democrats in his state, but who sees the GOP as an existential threat, "They want to destroy the country," he told me, "just start with data centers, they just seem to serve these corporations."

Dan is skeptical that Tafoya and Demuth can pull of the upsets, and gave me one pretty compelling reason why when he pointed a table of about 8 people, various ages, in their purple and gold and finery, saying, "I promise you every person at that table is a Republican, how many do you think will vote?"

"Three," I replied, "Maybe four?" To which he simply said, "Bingo."

The flipside to Dan’s turnout argument were the two or three dozen volunteers stomping the suburb for the GOP even as we spoke, and having that kind of ground game as early as September is typically something you see from Democrats, not from Republicans.

Over the next several weeks, the key question will be whether Minnesota Republicans, and fed-up independents, really believe they can win this time, after decades of Democrat dominance, if they do, and all signs point to yes, then expect a nail-biter in the Land of 10,000 Lakes coming this November.

This column will be in Minnesota for the rest of this week, looking to find out if a red dawn is really rising in Minnesota.

item.title: Man scales locked gate in chilling video after allegedly chasing college student home, then walks free: police
item.description: Security video shows a man scaling a locked gate to follow a UC Berkeley student into her apartment complex after allegedly chasing her home.
item.content:encoded:
Chilling surveillance video shows a UC Berkeley student racing through a locked gate as a homeless man allegedly chased her home, only to watch him scale the barrier, enter her apartment complex and remain free while prosecutors decide whether to charge him.

The frightening Sept. 15 encounter was captured on security video outside the apartment building in Berkeley, California.

The video shows the woman entering the secured complex around 8 p.m. Seconds later, a man climbs over the locked gate and allegedly follows her inside while holding an object initially reported as a knife.

VIRAL VIDEO OF HOMELESS ENCAMPMENT AROUND CITY OF BERKELEY SPARKS SAFETY CONCERNS FROM PARENT

Berkeley police later determined the object was likely a barbecue lighter and said there was no direct contact between the man and the woman.

The student, identified only as Eden for safety reasons, told ABC7 she had been walking her dog on Berkeley Way when the man made strange gestures, approached her and then began running toward her.

She made it inside the complex and reached an elevator before he could see where she went, according to the outlet.

"I shut the gate behind me, heard him and saw him climbing the gate," Eden told ABC7.

UCLA SORORITIES HIRE PRIVATE SECURITY AMID TERRIFYING HARASSMENT BY HOMELESS MEN: REPORT

The Berkeley Police Department said it received the woman’s call at approximately 8:04 p.m. Patrol officers were handling other high-priority emergencies at the time, including a domestic violence case and a report involving a missing person considered at risk.

Eden told ABC7 that officers arrived about an hour later but were unable to locate the man.

The next night, at approximately 9:24 p.m., police received another call reporting that the same man was lying on a sidewalk near Berkeley Way and Walnut Street.

Officers responded, detained and identified him, according to the department. Police confirmed that he was the person involved in the previous night’s alleged trespassing but did not arrest him.

FEDERAL JUDGE TIES ICE AGENTS' HANDS WITH RULING ON WARRANTLESS SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA ARRESTS

The department said California law generally prevents officers from making a warrantless arrest for a misdemeanor that did not occur in their presence. Because the alleged trespassing had happened the day before, officers said they could not arrest the man based solely on that offense.

Instead, investigators submitted the case to the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office for review. Prosecutors will determine whether criminal charges should be filed.

ABC7 reported that the district attorney’s office confirmed it was reviewing the case and that no charges had been filed as of Monday.

Eden said she was stunned a man could allegedly chase her into a secured building and still walk away after police identified him. She called for stronger laws and greater protections for residents, according to the outlet.

UC Berkeley and the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

item.title: Popular weight-loss drugs face numerous lawsuits over rare ‘eye stroke’ linked to vision loss
item.description: Hundreds of consumers allege GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy caused NAION, a rare eye stroke linked to sudden, often permanent vision loss.
item.content:encoded:
Hundreds of consumers are suing the manufacturers of GLP-1 receptor agonists, alleging the medications may increase the risk of a rare form of vision loss.

The patients behind the lawsuits allege that the medications caused NAION (nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy), according to The Wall Street Journal.

NAION is a rare eye condition in which blood flow to the optic nerve is suddenly reduced, leading to sudden vision loss.

POPULAR GLP-1 WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DEADLY BRAIN DISORDER

It is the most common cause of acute optic nerve injury in adults over age 50, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology and the National Eye Institute, which describes it as an "eye stroke."

"The problem with NAION is there's no treatment," Dr. Douglas Lazzaro, an ophthalmologist at NYU Langone Health, told Fox News Digital. "So it can cause some very profound vision loss."

The companies in question, Novo Nordisk (maker of Ozempic and Wegovy) and Eli Lilly (maker of Mounjaro and Zepbound), have disputed the allegations, according to the WSJ report.

POPULAR ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION DRUG LINKED TO EYE DISEASE THAT CAN CAUSE IRREVERSIBLE VISION LOSS

Novo Nordisk called the lawsuits meritless and pointed to company-funded research finding no increased risk of NAION with its drugs. Eli Lilly said it continues to monitor safety data and maintained that current studies do not prove GLP-1 medications cause the condition.

Fox News Digital reached out to the companies requesting comment.

Most of the published research to date has examined semaglutide, rather than tirzepatide.

In a data analysis of 37 million adults published in JAMA Ophthalmology in 2025, researchers found that people using semaglutide experienced a modest increase in NAION risk compared to people taking SGLT2 inhibitors, another class of diabetes medication.

DOCTORS REVEAL HIDDEN DANGER FOR SOME OZEMPIC, WEGOVY USERS WITH BRAIN DISORDERS

A 2024 Harvard Medical School study, published in the same journal, found that patients with type 2 diabetes who were prescribed semaglutide had approximately a fourfold higher relative risk of developing NAION. The absolute risk remained very low.

The authors of both studies noted that the research was observational and could not prove that the medication caused NAION. They emphasized that more evidence is needed.

The FDA has said it is reviewing available evidence regarding a possible association between semaglutide and NAION. The agency has not concluded that semaglutide causes NAION and has not issued a safety warning for semaglutide medications.

The European Medicines Agency concluded there is sufficient evidence of a possible association to recommend adding NAION as a "very rare" adverse reaction to semaglutide product information in Europe.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Lazzaro agreed that "whether or not that's statistically significant is hard to assess, because there were so many variables in this and it's hard to exactly match patients."

"But when they removed all of what they felt were confounding variables… how obese were the patients, male versus female, age, hypertension, level of obesity… they did find that there was a higher risk of NAION."

NAION typically causes sudden, painless vision loss in one eye, per the AAO. Other symptoms may include blurred or dim vision, loss of peripheral vision or decreased color vision.

Symptoms tend to develop first thing in the morning after waking up.

The biggest risk factors for the condition include age, diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, obstructive sleep apnea and smoking. As many people taking GLP-1 drugs have diabetes or obesity, some of these underlying risk factors could be factors in vision issues, experts note.

Diabetes itself is a well-established risk factor for NAION, making it difficult for observational studies to separate the effects of the disease from those of the medication, experts have noted.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Vision loss from NAION is often permanent. While some patients may regain partial vision over time, there is no proven treatment that can reverse the optic nerve damage.

The condition is rare, with roughly two to 10 cases per 100,000 people each year, depending on the population studied.

Experts emphasize that patients should not stop taking a prescribed GLP-1 medication without first speaking with their healthcare provider. For many people with diabetes or obesity, the medications' proven benefits may outweigh any potential vision risk.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

When discussing NAION, one important factor is what doctors call a "disc at risk," referring to certain characteristics of the optic disc, or optic nerve.

"So if I had a patient who had what I would see on exam is a disk at risk, a very compact optic nerve where everything's crowded, I would tell that patient probably to not go on a semaglutide," Lazzaro advised.

"My overall take on the matter is there's probably a slightly increased risk of NAION when using the semaglutides, but I think the health benefits outweigh the risks," he went on. 

"And unless I have a patient with a disk at risk, I would probably tell them to go on them if they're going to be a lot healthier from an overall standpoint."

item.title: Federal judge temporarily blocks deportation of illegal immigrant shot by ICE agent in Austin, attorney says
item.description: A federal judge has reportedly blocked the deportation of Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, who was shot by ICE in Austin during a Sunday confrontation.
item.content:encoded:
A federal judge has blocked the deportation of an illegal immigrant shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Austin over the weekend, his attorney said.

Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, who represents him, said her office has filed a federal lawsuit on behalf of her client, 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez. A judge ordered that Perez be present for a Sept. 30 hearing.

"That means Wilber cannot be deported in the meantime," Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote on Facebook. "For now, we have secured a temporary block on his deportation while his case moves forward."

SOCIALIST, COMMUNIST GROUPS COORDINATE, PROMOTE 'SPONTANEOUS' ANTI-ICE PROTESTS IN AUSTIN

She added that Perez still requires medical care and "we will continue fighting to protect his rights." He is still in "a lot of pain" and the bullet that struck him is still lodged in his body, she said.

Perez, a Venezuelan citizen, was delivering a DoorDash order when he made a U-turn under the highway before ICE agents continued to pursue him.

BRANDON GILL UNLOADS ON DEMOCRATS OVER ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH RAPING TEEN: 'COLLATERAL DAMAGE'

"The truck chased him and sideswiped him again. And the agents came out and shot him in the back of the neck and pulled him out of the car," Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

Perez had a final order of removal, authorities said. However, Lincoln-Goldfinch said her client received a removal order after a notice for his immigration hearing was sent to his old address, despite him having updated his address with the court.

FEDERAL APPEALS COURT COMPARES TRUMP MIGRANT DETENTION POLICY TO JAPANESE AMERICAN INTERNMENT

Travis County District Attorney Jose Garza sent a letter Tuesday to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin and ICE Director David Venturella asking that Garces Perez be allowed to remain in the United States pending an investigation into the shooting.

Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, and more than 100 other members of Congress also signed a letter to Mullin and Venturella demanding that Perez be released from ICE detention so he can receive medical treatment.

ICE OFFICER PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO LYING ABOUT MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING INVOLVING VENEZUELAN MAN

The lawmakers also asked that state authorities and law enforcement preserve all evidence from the shooting.

"Mr. Garces Perez is a key witness to this shooting, and given ICE's history of obscuring the facts in similar investigations, he must not be removed," the letter said.

DOJ CHARGES ICE OFFICER WITH LYING TO INVESTIGATORS FOLLOWING MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING OF VENEZUELAN MAN

The ICE officer who shot Perez is a new recruit to the agency but has years of law enforcement experience, including with the U.S. Border Patrol, sources told Fox News.

In addition, that unidentified officer wasn't wearing a body camera at the time of the shooting, multiple federal law enforcement sources told Fox News. ICE is supposed to have every officer equipped with cameras by the end of the month.

The officer completed the agency’s 256-hour Deportation Officer Training Program in August 2025 before undergoing additional operational and legal instruction through 2026, records show.

According to training logs, the officer scored 99.2% on his pistol qualification and completed coursework on use-of-force scenarios, as well as less-lethal tactics involving Tasers, OC spray, and batons.

His curriculum also included field operations training and practical exercises covering the entire custody continuum, alongside instruction on warrantless arrests, Title 19 authority, escort and removal procedures, expedited removal and custody procedures.

ICE AGENTS IN FATAL HOUSTON SHOOTING WERE NOT WEARING BODY CAMERAS, SOURCES SAY

Fox News Digital has reached out to ICE and the Department of Homeland Security.

In the wake of the shooting, multiple Democrats have criticized ICE, calling it a "rogue" agency that was "terrorizing our cities and threatening the safety of our residents."

Meanwhile, on Tuesday, DHS released a list of some illegal immigrants in Texas who have been arrested for various crimes, including supporting an Islamic State-inspired mass shooting on election day in 2024 and two Mexican citizens wanted for multiple murders in their native country.

item.title: Kristi Noem takes heat after bagging a massive elk & Keely Hodgkinson's sexy new speedsuit is a talker
item.description: Kristi Noem bags a massive elk on a Wyoming archery hunt and fires back at online critics, while Keely Hodgkinson debuts Nike's new speedsuit.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

We did it, friends. We made it to fall.

Now, I know Joe Kinsey tried to convince you in this morning's Screencaps that preferring autumn to summer is some sort of psy-op. That pumpkin spice is the devil's cocaine.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

But, respectfully, that just sounds like the opinion of someone who lives in northern Ohio. For those of us suffering in the ungodly heat and 400% humidity of the American South, sweater weather can't come soon enough.

In fact, today is the first time in nearly a month (26 days) that the temperature hasn't surpassed 90 degrees.

I mean, it's still 85. But baby steps.

Fun fact: just last week, the largest heat dome on planet Earth was centered right over my home state of Tennessee. I'll let this guy tell you all about it:

In other words, it's been miserable.

Man, I'm doing so much whining you'd think I was Caleb Williams pulling a hamstring.

Point is, I am positively giddy about dropping temperatures, changing leaves, fall hiking and not drowning in a vat of my own sweat. Hell, I might even burn a pumpkin candle — just to get all the haters riled up.

Speaking of haters, welcome to Tuesday Nightcaps, where Kristi Noem is taking some online heat for killing an animal. (Not her dog this time, thank God.)

But first, we're talking running fashion.

Buckle in, kids, and let's do this thing.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Keely Hodgkinson — an Olympic middle distance runner for Team Great Britain, in case you didn't know — turned some heads at the season-ending Athlos meet in North London on Friday. That's because, while all the other runners were decked out in their standard tiny bottoms and tanks, Keely rolled up in an all black, full-body catsuit.

Excuse me, it's a "zero-distraction speed suit," according to Nike.

But, respectfully, it was a little distracting. Just check out the aerodynamics on that thing!

I personally feel a little vindicated by Keely's look. In the handful of distance races I've done, the "serious" runners always say to me, "How do you run in leggings?!" As if I might as well tape concrete blocks to my feet while I'm at it.

And my answer is always the same: how do you NOT run in leggings?

See, the way my thighs are set up, running long distance in a pair of shorty shorts would just mean punching a one-way ticket to Chafe-town.

Granted, I'm just a casual neighborhood runner — not an Olympic sprinter. So what do I know?

This reminds me of that time a couple of years ago when Nike debuted its Team USA track and field kits for the Paris Olympics. The internet freaked out over the "sexist" designs meant to sexualize female track and field athletes instead of equipping them with comfortable and appropriate attire to compete.

Turns out, though, what actually happened is that Nike offered the women about 20 different combinations of a uniform — with tops and bottoms of various lengths. The ladies even had the option of wearing the men's kit if it would make them more comfortable.

It just so happens, though, that nearly all the female athletes chose to wear the tiny bikini and sports bra combo. So the outrage was entirely overblown. As social media outrage tends to be.

I digress.

Keely is having none of those front-wedgie-inducing underwears. And I don't blame her one bit.

She won the women's 800-meter event wearing that catsuit, by the way. So she might be onto something.

It's been a rough year for ol' Kristi Noem. First, she was ousted from her role as DHS Secretary. And then came those um... unflattering photos of her husband.

Kristi got knocked down. But in the spirit of Chumbawamba, she got up again.

And now, she's bagged a massive elk on an archery hunting trip in Wyoming.

I can't show you the picture of her and the actual elk because Instagram has deemed it too graphic for embeds. But you can see the gigantic animal she harvested here if you're interested.

EVA SHOCKEY SAYS WOMEN DON'T HAVE TO ABANDON THEIR FEMININITY TO BELONG IN THE OUTDOORS

You really have to toe the line with hunting content on Instagram. You can post all the dead fish photos you want, but as soon as you show a mammal down, it becomes a whole thing.

Last week, I posted a cute little video of NASCAR driver Chase Briscoe talking about his 4-year-old son's love of hunting on OutKick OutDoors. Instagram finally allowed it, but it got shadow banned on YouTube and removed from TikTok for "violating community guidelines."

Annoying.

Predictably, Kristi has gotten plenty of hate in the comments for harvesting this big, beautiful bull elk. And yes, probably from the same people who have no problem grabbing a Big Mac from the McDonald's drive-thru. Because as long as you don't have to actually see the dead animal you're eating, you can delude yourself into believing you have the moral high ground.

Kristi put the critics in their place, calling them "ignorant and uninformed."

"Of course this beautiful animal will nourish our family and many others we will share with," she wrote.

"These majestic animals are incredible and I’ve so loved learning their ways from my father, sharing memories in the mountains with him and my brothers and now my friends."

Kristi concluded: "Shame on you who desecrate and don’t understand the stewardship responsibilities God has given us. Go to a store and shop for anything that hasn’t been harvested and you will find bare shelves and your family will starve."

Anyway, who wants elk burgers?

Let's open the mailbag.

📩 Email: amber.harding@outkick.com (Send your thoughts, stories, tips, rants and photos of your dog.)

🐦 Twitter/X: @TheAmberHarding

📸 Instagram: @amberharding

Last week, we talked about how some losers (unsuccessfully) tried to cancel Ella Langley after some old photos resurfaced of her deer hunting in Alabama.

Gary B. writes: The state of NJ has such an over population of deer that the hunting season has been extended. They are destroying the ecosystem. The season starts October 3rd and me and my brother are tracking a massive buck on his property in the southern Pine Barrens. His son got a large buck last year and hopefully that trend will continue.

As far as the WNBA, basketball in general sucks. The game went south when they added the 3 point line. Basketball used to almost be as physical as football or hockey. You had to control the paint it was an inside game of strength. Now they shoot soon as they cross the half court line. The only basketball I watch is college hoops in the month of March. That's awesome but then again college sports are in my opinion better then the professional level mainly because of the intensity of the crowd . Texas and Ohio State proves my point. 

Nikki S. writes: Love Ella and all the hate only shows she’s "made it." Unfortunately that’s the world we live in today. And btw pretty sure the majority of Ella’s fan base was raised where hunting and fishing were both recreation and a source of food.

Steve B. writes: The idiot who thinks hunting is a moral  problem,  has never gone to a slaughterhouse or feedlot to see how his porterhouse steak is actually created.

John G. writes: I have the pain and joy of watching this teams since founding when Wilson was the coach and his son was the QB. Been thru the the perfect season. Also attended their first game in now named Hard Rock stadium when the team was owned by the "Garbage Man".

So I have seen the highlights and low lights.

They will be back maybe not this year but eventually. I just hope they don't capture Detroit's record.

Amber:

Listen, if you're gonna tank, TANK.

None of this 6-11, 5-12 crap. I'm expecting a full buy-in from team personnel: No. 1 draft pick or bust, baby.

"The memo is pretty clear that there's a serious issue there that shows different reasons why that plea might not have been accepted," Kohberger's new attorney, Greg Rauch, told Fox News Digital. "Those issues have to be flushed out and explored.

Although the memo's Tuesday release appeared to have surprised him, he said he initially filed it under seal out of an abundance of caution and to avoid running afoul of previous orders in the case. 

Kohberger, a 31-year-old former criminology Ph.D. student, is serving four consecutive sentences of life in prison without the possibility of parole, plus another 10 years. Rauch was assigned to his case over the summer and did not represent him as it initially played out.

"Before June 26, [2025,] the Court knew that counsel was asking for additional time not only to review evidence and continue investigation, but also to investigate Kohberger’s ability to rationally understand and make consequential decisions and to obtain expert assistance in communicating with him about whether to resolve the case short of trial," Rauch wrote to the court in a document that remained sealed for nearly a month.

"The Court disagrees that the information contained in the Supplemental Memorandum is intimate, protected or will result in harm if disclosed," Hippler wrote. "It simply describes in very general terms trial counsel's concerns about Petitioner's difficulty in comprehending adverse rulings and understanding their effect on the outcome of the case."

IDAHO JUDGE GRANTS BRYAN KOHBERGER TWO HEARINGS NEXT YEAR AS ADMITTED KILLER SEEKS TO WITHDRAW GUILTY PLEA

Kohberger's former defense team, led by Anne Taylor, had sought more time for discovery as his trial approached last year. According to the unsealed filing, they were also quietly seeking help for Kohberger to understand the proceedings.

"The Court thereafter denied the requested additional time," Rauch wrote. "The sealed June 26 Order rejected the need for further investigation and concluded overall that Kohberger had not demonstrated good cause for a continuance or prejudice from proceeding to trial as scheduled."

item.title: Dem AG running for higher office dodges questions on bid to free man who killed pregnant woman
item.description: Nevada AG and governor candidate, Aaron Ford, ducked questions about his decision to back early release for a man who killed a pregnant woman while out on bond for a series of other violent crimes.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Nevada's Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford is refusing to explain why he personally backed a clemency bid for a convicted killer who took the life of a pregnant woman while out on bail for a series of armed robbery attacks on Vegas tourists, dodging questions on camera as he campaigns to be the state's next governor.

State records in Nevada show Ford was listed as the sole sponsor for Norman Smith’s commutation application at a Sept. 16 Nevada Board of Pardons Commissioners meeting. Smith was serving time for killing a pregnant woman in a convenience store parking lot—a crime committed while he was out on bail for a series of armed robbery attempts committed against Vegas Strip tourists, according to court documents and local reporting at the time. 

Despite Ford's backing, the board ultimately denied the clemency bid, while Ford skipped the commutation hearing that was scheduled and later walked away from a questioner asking him to justify the decision to sponsor Smith's application at a Las Vegas airport.

Ford's sponsorship of the convicted killer's early release bid comes as he mounts a gubernatorial run against Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, who has repeatedly attacked the attorney general's record on public safety and criminal justice reform. 

WHITE HOUSE DENIES TRUMP INFLUENCED BY 'PARDON BROKERS' AFTER '60 MINUTES' INVESTIGATION

When confronted about the sponsorship, Ford's campaign told Fox News Digital the attorney general missed the hearing due to an out-of-state family medical emergency and argued that sponsoring an application is merely a routine procedural step allowing the Board of Pardons to decide on a specific clemency request—but the campaign repeatedly refused to explain why Ford chose to elevate Smith's specific case.

"Are you Aaron Ford?" a conservative tracker asked the gubernatorial candidate as he deplaned in Las Vegas after flying to Arizona, the same day as Smith's Sept. 16 commutation hearing.

"I am," Ford replied to the tracker, who went on to tell the Nevada Attorney General that she has been "following his stuff" on social media. "Nice to meet you."

The tracker continued with small talk until pivoting to a question about the decision to sponsor Smith's clemency bid.

"I have a question, are you—you're sponsoring Norman Smith's pardon, right?"

BIDEN CLEMENCY BLITZ LEFT DOJ SCRAMBLING AS MANY COMMUTATONS BYPASSED NORMAL VETTING, EMAILS SHOW

"Uhh, don't know which one you're talking about, but anyway—good to see you," Ford responded before shuffling away with his wife following their trip to visit their college-aged son who was said to be sick. Fox News Digital pressed Ford's team on what his son was facing in terms of an ailment but was not provided an answer.

"Is there a reason why you're pardoning him?" Ford was asked as he attempted to skirt away from the questioner.

"Good to see you," was Ford's response before walking away. "Take care."

"No reason?" the tracker doubled down.

CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM

Under Nevada Board of Pardons Commissioners rules, an inmate’s clemency application sits in a queue until one of the board’s nine members—which includes the governor, attorney general, and state Supreme Court justices—chooses to officially sponsor it. By sponsoring Smith’s application, Ford elevated the case out of the administrative queue and onto the official state agenda for a full hearing and vote.

Based on a Fox News Digital review of official meeting agendas from 2026, Smith’s application was the only commutation request sponsored by Ford all year.

In 2015, Smith was free on bail and facing 14 charges in connection with a series of armed robbery attacks on Vegas Strip tourists when he shot and killed the pregnant woman, Tineshea Adams, according to court documents and reporting at the time from the Las Vegas Review-Journal. Court documents show Smith, who was initially charged with murder but was eventually convicted of voluntary manslaughter and three counts of armed robbery, claimed the killing was the result of self-defense. Smith is currently serving a 10-to-39-year prison sentence.

Republican political strategist Matt Gorman slammed Ford's silent airport exit, telling Fox News Digital that the attorney general's refusal to answer speaks volumes.

"Aaron Ford was moving faster through that airport than the violent criminals he’s trying to put back on the street," Gorman said. "If Nevada's top law enforcement officer can't even explain why he backed early release for a man who killed a pregnant woman while out on bail for a series of other violent crimes, he has no business asking voters to make him governor."

item.title: Spanberger's data center plan on collision course with her party's green energy push, critics warn
item.description: Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger's data center plan restricts natural gas generation while demanding grid reliability, raising questions about the gap.
item.content:encoded:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger's data center plan is facing criticism that one of its key provisions may work against itself.

Limits on on-site natural gas generation could make it harder, not easier, for large data centers to support Virginia's already-stressed electric grid.

The stakes are high because Virginia is already struggling to keep up with rapidly growing data center electricity demand, especially in Northern Virginia, where demand is outpacing the expansion of transmission lines and substations. 

Restricting on-site natural gas generation could make it harder for large data centers to add dependable power at a time when the state is trying to stabilize the grid while also shifting toward cleaner energy sources.

WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE

"Everyone recognizes the need for changes in how Virginia engages with data centers. But the governor’s proposal is internally contradictory and raises serious questions about whether it can actually work," Virginia House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore told Fox News Digital.

Spanberger’s Data Center Accountability Framework calls for data centers to help stabilize the electric grid while limiting the amount of electricity they can generate from on-site natural gas.

Kilgore, R-Gate City, noted that the plan states data centers should source their "own clean power" while at the same time seeking to "limit the amount of electricity data centers can generate from … natural gas."

The plan also calls for accelerated clean energy development and prioritizes grid access for data centers that invest in "clean energy" or "further limit on-site natural gas generation."

"And if they fail to meet the governor’s preferred energy standards, they could face higher taxes," Kilgore said.

"What reliable, dispatchable source of power is supposed to fill the gap? That’s not a political question: it’s how the grid works."

A Spanberger spokesperson told Fox News Digital the governor's plan is the "most comprehensive and wide-ranging" in the country and that it aims to protect both Virginia residents and the commonwealth's "natural beauty."

"The governor’s plan also ends secrecy around data centers by banning non-disclosure agreements and strengthening local approval," the spokesperson said.

"While Gov. Spanberger is pushing to hold data centers accountable — an action polling shows is overwhelmingly supported by Democrats and Republicans — the Trump administration has continued to dismiss the very real concerns Virginians have about data centers’ energy, water and land usage."

Spanberger’s plan can still allow data centers to construct on-site power because the framework only restricts the use of that power.

She also signed a bill by Del. Rip Sullivan, D-Great Falls, that sharply increased Virginia's goals for energy storage, including a target of 1,600 megawatts of storage capacity at homes and businesses.

TEXAS GOV. GREG ABBOTT EFFECTIVELY PAUSES NEW DATA CENTER PROJECTS PENDING STATEWIDE GRID AUDIT

Republicans said they found some common ground with Spanberger on the issue, citing public unease about the explosion in data center construction and stress on resources.

"I am glad the governor is finally talking about high power bills and data centers. Virginians already are," Senate Minority Leader Ryan McDougle, R-Hanover, said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital. "This should not be a partisan issue."

But he also echoed Kilgore’s concern about the plan’s energy-generation dynamics amid looming zero-emissions requirements.

"Virginians — Democrats, Republicans and Independents — will tell you the same thing. Their power bills went up. The laws raising electric bills — the tax on carbon, the Virginia Clean Economy Act, solar mandates, and more — should be repealed, and the companies building data centers should pay their own costs," McDougle said.

At the same time, some top Democrats criticized their governor’s plan.

"The governor is finally feeling the heat but still ignoring the fire," Senate President Pro-Tem L. Louise Lucas told Richmond’s ABC affiliate.

Lucas, Portsmouth, said the framework wrongly ignored the need to end tax exemptions for the centers.

The debate comes as Virginia is already in the midst of a state-mandated transition away from carbon-emitting electricity generation under the Virginia Clean Economy Act.

Under the law, the state’s major utilities generally must retire their remaining in-state generating units that emit carbon by burning fuel by the end of 2045. The law also allows utilities to seek relief from those requirements if compliance would threaten the reliability or security of electric service.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Spanberger’s new framework would push qualifying data centers further in that direction, limiting on-site natural gas generation while prioritizing grid access for facilities that invest in clean energy, reduce backup generator emissions and further restrict their reliance on natural gas.

Kilgore’s argument raised new tension. Restricting one source of on-site power before sufficient dependable alternatives are available could create the very reliability challenge Spanberger’s framework says it is intended to prevent.

The issue is particularly acute in Northern Virginia, where data center electricity demand is growing faster than the transmission lines and substations needed to serve it can be expanded, according to Loudoun County.

In Northern Virginia’s so-called data center alley, officials are already troubleshooting how to stabilize the grid as an explosion in data center construction puts massive sites among densely populated subdivisions.

There, Loudoun County leaders say the typical data center requires a continuous supply of 30 to 200 megawatts, enough to otherwise power 200,000 average homes.

The county’s explanation of data center development considerations also specifically lists "natural gas reciprocating engines" as one of the avenues for on-site power, appearing to contradict the push by the governor away from the fuel source.

Fox News Digital reached out to Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., for additional comment on the matter because he represents the county in Congress and has been a leading voice in the data center debate.

Earlier this month, Subramanyam introduced the National Data Center Plan, which would similarly require data centers to pay for their own energy, analyze their effects on the community, environment and national security before beginning construction.

The debate leaves the central dispute over Spanberger’s data center plan unresolved on whether clean generation, battery storage and flexible demand can provide enough dependable power to accommodate Virginia’s rapidly growing data center load as the state simultaneously restricts on-site natural gas generation.

item.title: Five top takeaways from Trump's high-stakes UN speech to the world
item.description: Trump told the United Nations General Assembly that Iran can make a deal or face annihilation, while celebrating the Greenland agreement with Denmark.
item.content:encoded:
"A lot has happened since we gathered here last year," President Donald Trump said midway through his address to the United Nations General Assembly.

No kidding. First there was the Gaza ceasefire and hostage return, then Operation Absolute Resolve that removed Nicolas Maduro from power in Venezuela, and, of course, the deployment of U.S. military and economic power to stop Iran’s "mad dash" for a nuclear weapon.

Trump has put American courage and fortitude on display by taking big risks to strengthen the U.S. position—not just for global leadership, but for America’s future. This U.N. speech had its triumphant moments. "Bully no more," Trump said as he touted the battlefield success of Operation Epic Fury. Yet Trump’s serious and formal tone was evidence that this has also been a year that has tested the optimism and tried the patience of both President Trump and the American people.

TRUMP DEFENDS US INTERVENTIONS ABROAD AHEAD OF 'BIG DECISION' ON IRAN: 'SETTLING YEARS OF UNFINISHED BUSINESS'

Here are five takeaways.

1. Iran’s Choice is a Deal or Annihilation. "Just imagine if such a vile regime were ever empowered to carry out large-scale terror attacks from behind a nuclear shield. This was the reality we had to confront—a reality that far too many preferred to ignore," Trump explained on Tuesday.

And the U.N. audience broke into spontaneous applause when Trump vowed again that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. He asked world leaders to stay "united in maintaining pressure" on Iran. But, to no one’s surprise, this speech was also a direct message to the "lunatic clerics" who run Iran, to borrow the phrase from Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

SECURITY EXPERT HAILS TRUMP'S GREENLAND PACT AS A 'BIG DEAL' ON PAR WITH ALASKA PURCHASE

Iran can make a deal or face annihilation. "I believe we’ll make a deal right after the midterms," Trump said. He’s ever-hopeful, but this is why 50,000 U.S. service members, led by two aircraft carriers, remain in the region under U.S. Central Command. Either way, he said, we "will soon see a world free of the 51-year menace." And indeed, it could go either way.

2. Greenland. Did you see Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen happily nodding during Trump’s remarks? Yes, this agreement that keeps Chinese investment out of Greenland and builds up Pituffik and other Space Force locations was a win-win for American security, Greenland, Denmark and NATO. This deal meant a lot to Trump, and it was smiling faces all around with the president, Frederiksen and Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen at the signing ceremony held immediately after his U.N. address.

TOP TRUMP OFFICIAL REVEALS HOW 30-MINUTE MILITARY OP UNLOCKED VENEZUELA OIL WINDFALL FOR US BUYERS

3. The Cartels in the Crosshairs. Trump’s speech delivered two scorching messages reiterating his commitment to the Western Hemisphere. First, Venezuela and the United States together control roughly 22% of the world’s proved oil reserves. Second, Trump said the "cartels are the ISIS of the Western Hemisphere" and decried these "sick, demented adversaries." Put this in perspective: These cartels control more cash than the global jihadis, so expect drug boat strikes to continue. "The United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere. And if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States," Trump warned.

4. Super Intelligence. Not content with renaming lakes, seas and the Kennedy Center, Trump said he wants AI to be called Super Intelligence—or SI. He joked about seeing whether "SI" catches on, but here’s the serious message: The U.S. is ahead of China and will do whatever it takes to achieve supremacy in the global race for tech stack adoption and market share. "Whoever wins SI wins," Trump reiterated. That’s a nice setup for the state visit of China’s Xi Jinping later this week.

TRUMP UNLOADS ON TECH TITANS PUSHING FOR SLOWDOWN ON EMERGING INDUSTRY: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’

5. Melania Trump. Considering how little the U.N. has done with Iran or, for that matter, Ukraine, Trump let it off easy. Trump took a few swipes at the U.N. bureaucracy, but he was also courteous about U.N. Resolution 2817 condemning Iran’s attacks on international shipping. Most of all, Trump took time to acknowledge his wife, Melania Trump. On March 2, 2026, she became the first sitting first lady to preside over a meeting of the U.N. Security Council, leading a discussion on children and technology. During the speech, the first lady was seated with Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. As Trump scanned the audience for her, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer waved to point her out.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

This was a thoughtful gesture, but it was poignant as well. For all the courageous tone, President Donald J. Trump has a lot of work ahead of him.

His 2026 U.N. speech may stand as the high-water mark of Trump’s bold efforts to improve international security and diminish the menace of China.

item.title: Reporter's Notebook: Congress struggles to find a message that resonates with voters ahead of midterms
item.description: Marshall McLuhan's "the medium is the message" frames a midterms fight where both parties struggle to sell voters on affordability and AI policy.
item.content:encoded:
Canadian sociologist Marshall McLuhan famously declared that "the medium is the message."

But what if the message is just "medium?" Or, perhaps in today’s vernacular, "mid."

Both sides are trying to curate what they say to voters to coax them to vote for their party in November.

"The message matters," House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., said on Fox. "We have accomplished a ton. No taxes on overtime. No taxes on tips. We raised the childcare tax credit. The list goes on and on."

EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE VANCE'S INTIMATE CAPITOL HILL HUDDLE AS REPUBLICANS CONFRONT TOUGH MIDTERM TERRAIN

Those are all vestiges of the "big, beautiful bill," which the Republican-led Congress passed last summer. Now Republicans are scrambling to remind voters what they did.

"It was a great message last year, and we missed the opportunity, in my view, to talk about the good things we did last year," Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., conceded.

But Cramer says voters want to know what you’ve done for them lately. And that’s where the GOP could struggle.

"People's rearview mirror is getting shorter and shorter all the time," said Cramer. "What you are going to do for me today is more important to them than what you tried to do a year ago."

That’s why some Republicans are frank about their prospects at the polls.

"This midterm is going to be a f---ing bloodbath," fumed Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., who is retiring. "I think that both parties know everyone's putting blame on the Republicans right now."

Democrats are campaigning on affordability. The cost of groceries and fuel are top of mind.

"What's most important to Americans are pocketbook issues," said Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va. "And they see the tariff strategy as punishing our allies and punishing their pocketbooks for no purpose."

But Democrats are also stumping on a promise.

"The top priority in these next two years is going to be holding Donald Trump accountable," said Colorado Democratic House nominee Melat Kiros.

"We'll hold this administration accountable for its corruption," House Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., warned.

"We will subpoena them if we need to," declared Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash.

It’s unclear if threats of presidential probes could dilute the Democrats’ directive this fall.

"When you talk about (investigations)," yours truly asked House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., "Does that step on your message in any way about costs?"

"No, because there's a cost to the American people around corruption," answered Jeffries. "Which is why the American people are demanding that action be taken and that we hold the crooks accountable."

FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS

Still, one Democrat says the party is better politically if it sticks to bread and butter issues.

"There are a lot of corruption questions," said Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt. "But I think the gold ring, the brass ring, is focusing on affordability."

While Republicans try to remind voters about the "big, beautiful bill," another prominent GOP senator says his party lacks a coherent message.

"We're lucky because the Democrats don't have a plan either," said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La. "Here's the strategy for both sides. ‘The other guys are worse than me.’"

So, some Republicans are reverting to a wedge issue that worked for them at the ballot box two years ago.

"We're going to tell the story about the closed border. I mean, President Trump has the most secure border in our history," argued Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala.

But both parties are evaluating a late-emerging issue: artificial intelligence.

"In the next 30 days, as we go into this election, Democrats have an opportunity to basically put AI on the ballot," Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., said on MS NOW.

Jeffries suggested Republicans are dismissing immediate concerns about AI agents going rogue.

"This is a serious thing. It requires urgent congressional action and Republicans are abandoning their responsibility," said Jeffries. "Democrats will not do that."

Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, faces a competitive race this fall in the Buckeye State. He tried to blend a sliver of concerns over AI with the "affordability" question last week.

The House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act, 417-3. The bill defrays the high utility costs consumers are sometimes forced to pay if they live near data centers. The legislation diverts those bills to Big Tech firms that run the data centers. So, Husted made the case to protect consumers from shelling out extra cash.

"If you create the cost, you should pay the cost," said Husted.

OBAMA PRIVATELY SOUNDS ALARM ON ‘DANGEROUS’ AI, URGES DEMOCRATS TO PUT ISSUE AT CENTER OF AGENDA

But Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., the top Democrat on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, stood in the way.

"It’s not enough for us to tell states to consider making data centers pay for grid updates rather than voluntary pledges or suggestions to states," said Heinrich. "Congress needs to pass real legislation with real teeth."

The New Mexico Democrat then objected, blocking Husted’s entreaty on the spot. However, Republicans actually think the move by Heinrich could boost Husted, help Republicans and backfire on Democrats. In other words, a Democratic blockade might assist the GOP make the point that they’re for affordability and the other party is standing in the way. Especially on a bill that passed with such overwhelming support in the House.

"Now there's a differentiation between Republicans and Democrats. Republicans are looking out for ratepayers. Democrats are not," said Cramer.

Fox is told it’s possible the Senate could try again on the data center-related measure before senators leave the Capitol for the midterms. Another on-the-spot, unanimous consent request would take a matter of minutes to either pass or block the bill (again). 

But a customary debate accompanied by multiple procedural votes likely consumes a week — even if there’s support for the plan. That said, some lawmakers from both sides wouldn’t mind a roll call vote where they’re documented as supporting the issue. Or a vote where Republicans dare Democrats to go on the record opposing it.

What that means is that the Senate likely leaves town for the midterms without addressing "affordability." Republicans can blame Democrats — a little. Specifically on the Ratepayer Protection Act. But Democrats aren’t in the majority. They can upbraid Republicans for not addressing some of those pocket book concerns.

That’s the "message" ahead of November. As Kennedy suggested, it might fall flat on both sides. Or, as is sometimes said these days, "mid."

After all, it is the midterms.

item.title: Red state Dem faces fury for suggesting illegal aliens should replace American workers
item.description: Hallie Shoffner said farmers would "trade five Americans just for one" illegal immigrant worker, drawing sharp criticism from Sen. Tom Cotton's campaign.
item.content:encoded:
A Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate from Arkansas is facing scrutiny for comments she recently made on a podcast suggesting that illegal alien workers are more valuable than their American counterparts.

"I want to talk about the fact that our immigration system is backlogged, bureaucratic and doesn't actually help anybody, including American employers who want folks who want to follow the law," Hallie Shoffner said on the "Free Arkansas Podcast" during an hour-long discussion about a wide spectrum of political issues.

Shoffner, a farmer, is running against Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark. in the deep red state.

DEM SENATE NOMINEE CHANGES TUNE ON ICE AFTER VOWING NOT 'ONE MORE DIME' FOR AGENCY

She continued by saying she had a discussion with a fellow farmer, who she said was a Republican, about foreign labor.

"Labor is a huge issue, especially when you don't have a large workforce," she said. "And every farmer will tell you, 'yeah, at one point we did, or still do, employ undocumented immigrants.'" And it's absolutely ridiculous that these folks are being rounded up because they're hardworking people. They're some of the best people we know."

"And honestly, we'd trade five Americans just for one of them because of how hard they work," she said.

Shoffner then demanded a pathway for illegal aliens to work in the United States legally, claiming "when they're good workers, we pay them well, they're good workers, they spend money here [and] they have family here."

Cotton's campaign accused Shoffner of implying that she has hired illegal aliens.

OMAR'S NEW LEGISLATION TARGETING ICE SPARKS OUTRAGE WHEN THE INTERNET SEES WHAT'S IN IT: 'UN-AMERICAN'

"Hallie Shoffner’s campaign isn’t denying that she employed illegal aliens," campaign spokesman James Arnold told Fox News Digital. "They’re also standing by Hallie Shoffner’s claim that just one illegal immigrant is more valuable than five American citizens."

"Every Democrat running for Congress needs to answer if they agree with Hallie Shoffner’s belief that illegal aliens are worth more than Americans," Arnold said.

In a response to Fox News Digital, Shoffner's campaign manager Anna-Lee Pittman said the candidate's comments were taken out of context, and accused Cotton of being unwilling to have a conversation to help "fix the immigration system."

Cotton, she said, "spends his days combing through video clips of Hallie Shoffner to find any possible inelegant phrase or line that he can chop up to misrepresent an hour-long conversation and present it with no context," noting that "[i]n this response, Shoffner relayed a conversation she had with another farmer about challenges with labor."

Shoffner once joined the chorus of left-wing calls to defund U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

DHS ISSUES SCATHING REBUKE AFTER FORMER ATLANTA MAYOR KEISHA LANCE BOTTOMS TOUTS CUTTING TIES WITH ICE

"I would vote to defund ICE as it exists right now," Shoffner said in an event June. "Immigration and Customs Enforcement was created not that long ago, and it no longer serves the purpose it was originally created for." 

"I would not spend one more dime on ICE, because — not just because of the human dignity issue — but also the fact that it is now the largest law enforcement agency in the country," she said. "It has 10 times the budget of the organization that fights child sex trafficking."

But in a Facebook post earlier this month, the red state Democratic candidate changed her tune.

"I don’t want to defund ICE, I want to reform it," she said.

Immigration is a hotbed issue heading into the midterm elections, as it was two years ago during President Donald Trump's campaign to occupy the White House for a second term.

The Trump administration has carried out immigration operations nationwide to arrest and deport illegal aliens, drawing blowback from Democrat politicians and activists.

Fox News Digital's Alex Miller contributed to this report.

item.title: AOC opens up about race, gender in weighing possible 2028 White House bid
item.description: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., opened up about how race and gender factor into her 2028 presidential election calculus in a new interview.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., raised concerns during an interview published Tuesday about how her race and gender could factor into a potential 2028 presidential bid.

"Pretty candidly, I think about my identity," Ocasio-Cortez said in an interview with The New York Times. "I’m not naïve to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina. And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities."

The progressive congresswoman said of a possible White House run, "I think about it personally."

"I am 36, I’m about to turn 37 years old — and what that means for my life," she added.

AOC, ASKED ABOUT RUNNING FOR PRESIDENT, SAYS HER AMBITION IS 'WAY BIGGER THAN THAT'

"This country has never elected a female president. Why are we pretending that this is not a factor?" she told the Times. "That doesn’t make it impossible, but to act as though it’s not a factor in anything ever is really a form of, like, denialism."

Ocasio-Cortez said the discussion around race and gender was often seen as a complaint or excuse.

"I often hesitate to even talk about it," she told the outlet, "because people then just register it as an excuse or a complaint."

"If you’re asking me about the things that I weigh, of course, that’s part of what I weigh," she told the Times of possibly running for president. "It’s funny because it’s kind of like, everyone else is allowed to talk about it, but I’m not?"

HASAN PIKER BRUSHES OFF DEMS WHO SEE HIM AS A LIABILITY, NAMES HIS '28 CHOICE

She argued people get defensive when gender is suggested as playing a role in electoral politics.

"I experience it tremendously — from the right and from the left," she told the Times.

Ocasio-Cortez has been generating 2028 buzz. LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic megadonor Reid Hoffman described the progressive firebrand as "pragmatic." Hoffman made the comments at Politico's Decoded Summit in September, and said former Vice President Kamala Harris would have a "very challenging path" to the nomination.

"It depends a little bit," Hoffman said when asked whether he would support Ocasio-Cortez for a 2028 run. "I think she's much more pragmatic than people give her credit for."

AOC’S PRIMARY WIN REIGNITES SPECULATION OVER 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID, SCHUMER CHALLENGE

Far-left streamer Hasan Piker said he would absolutely campaign for AOC should she decide to run in 2028.

Ocasio-Cortez topped a July poll from the University of New Hampshire Granite State. In the poll, AOC was one point ahead of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and 17 points ahead of Harris.

The polling average as of Sept. 22, according to the New York Times, has Harris leading with 27%, followed by Gov. Gavin Newsom at 16%, Buttigieg with 10%, and Ocasio-Cortez also at 10%.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Judy Pino, advisor on Hispanic issues and a Spanish-language spokesperson for Independent Women and The LIBRE Initiative, reacted to Ocasio-Cortez' remarks in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Pino said, "Whether America is ready for a Latina president isn’t the question. As a Latina, I find that framing beside the point and, frankly, insulting." 

"It reduces a serious debate about the future of this country to gender and ethnicity when Americans are worried about whether they can afford groceries, buy a home, grow a business, and create a better future for their children," she continued. 

Pino said Ocasio-Cortez "identifies" with democratic socialism, and argued, "we should believe candidates when they tell us what they stand for."

"For many Latinos, that debate has particular resonance. Families from Cuba, Venezuela and elsewhere in Latin America have witnessed governments embrace socialism while expanding state control and restricting economic and political freedom. Those experiences help explain why the word ‘socialism’ can carry consequences far beyond a political slogan for some Latino families,' Pino said in the statement. 

Pino said Latino voters were more focused on AOC's policies rather than her gender or ethnicity. 

"That's the debate America should be having: not whether we're ready for a Latina president, but whether Americans want to move this country in a socialist direction," she said.

item.title: Will Levis to sign with New York Jets practice squad in hopes of meeting potential under respected QB coaches
item.description: Will Levis signs with the New York Jets practice squad after being waived by the Tennessee Titans, joining an offensive staff led by Frank Reich.
item.content:encoded:
Will Levis is back in the NFL and hoping to relaunch a career that crashed and burned with the Tennessee Titans by going to a more successful team that can offer him an environment in which he can learn, improve and thrive:

The New York Jets?

Hey, it's an opportunity.

AARON GLENN'S JETS BET ON GENO SMITH AND FRANK REICH TO ESCAPE AFC EAST BASEMENT IN 2026

Levis is signing with the Jets practice squad, per multiple reports. The Jets are expected to release Bailey Zappe in a corresponding move.

And, no, this doesn't mean the Jets are planning to replace Geno Smith as their starter. But the club doesn't exactly have a star sitting behind Smith in rookie Cade Klubnik and it doesn't hurt to have an experienced young vet with some potential in the pipeline.

That's what Levis is now. Experienced. And potentially good as long as he figures out how to stop being the player who was released by the Tennessee Titans after they gave up on him.

Levis entered the NFL as one of the 2023 draft’s most intriguing quarterback prospects, but also one of its biggest mysteries.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Tennessee selected the Kentucky standout in the second round (No. 33 overall) after he failed to meet his own expectations of being selected in the first round.

Levis made an immediate impression in his first start, throwing four touchdown passes in a victory over Atlanta. But his rookie season was interrupted by an ankle injury. And it never really got better after that.

Levis finished his rookie year with flashes of arm strength and playmaking ability, while leaving the Titans hopeful they had found their long-term quarterback.

But, nope.

That optimism in Tennessee disappeared during a 2024 season in which Levis struggled with turnovers, sacks and consistency. He threw 13 touchdown passes that season, which wasn't enough to lift the Titans to any significant degree.

And he threw 12 interceptions, which was a cause of great frustration.

The team, which was not good to begin with, was 2–10 in the games Levis started.

And then things actually got worse.

Levis suffered a right shoulder injury against Miami that continued to bother him and ultimately required offseason surgery, costing him the entire 2025 season. After Tennessee selected Cam Ward with the No. 1 overall pick in 2025, Levis’ future with the franchise was sealed.

The Titans waived him in August.

So now what?

He's 27 years old and needs coaching. The Jets have the coaching experience and prowess to help a quarterback needing work.

Offensive coordinator Frank Reich was Peyton Manning's quarterback coach when Manning won an MVP award and then a Super Bowl the following year. He coached Philip Rivers in both San Diego and Indianapolis. And he coached Andrew Luck one year when Luck threw 39 TD passes.

Jets quarterback coach Bill Musgrave forged a history with Matt Ryan when he was drafted by the Atlanta Falcons and was Derek Carr's offensive coordinator when the QB went to consecutive Pro Bowls in 2015 and '16.

None of this means Levis is the future quarterback in New York. The Jets are not exactly a patient nor stable organization.

But getting some good coaching is something that will benefit Levis as he tries to live up to his potential.

His NFL journey now enters a critical second chapter: Levis remains only 27 and possesses legitimate arm talent, but he must convince another team that his decision-making, health and poise can catch up with his physical gifts.
